in_context.text: Paul is pleading with Philemon for Onesimus, who had become Paul's spiritual son while Paul was in prison. He admits that Onesimus was once "unprofitable" to Philemon, but says he is now "profitable" to both of them. Paul then sends him back and asks Philemon to receive him as a brother.

speaker.text: Paul, writing as "a prisoner of Jesus Christ" together with Timothy.

audience.text: Philemon, Paul's fellow-worker, along with Apphia, Archippus, and the church that met in his house.

affected.text: Onesimus, Philemon's servant. He had left Philemon and had become a believer through Paul.

what.text: Paul contrasts Onesimus's past and present. Before, he was useless to Philemon. Now he is useful to Philemon and to Paul. This change supports Paul's request that Philemon take him back.

events.text: This happened after Onesimus had "departed" from Philemon and come to faith through Paul during Paul's imprisonment. Onesimus was being sent back at the time of the letter.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 60-62, from prison in Rome, at the same time as Colossians. Scholarly view: nearly all accept that Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul wrote from prison, but the letter does not name the city. Rome is the traditional view. It was sent to Philemon's household, probably in Colossae, since Colossians calls Onesimus "one of you."

purpose.text: The verse helps Paul's appeal. If Onesimus is now useful, Philemon has good reason to welcome him back. Paul even says he would have liked to keep him to serve with him.

big_picture.text: The "in time past... but now" pattern matches other Scripture, where God's mercy changes people: "Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God." It also echoes the father's words about the son who "was lost, and is found."

for_readers.text: A person's past does not have to define how believers receive them now. Paul asks that Onesimus, once "unprofitable," be received as "a brother beloved"; Mark too became "profitable... for the ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11).

why_it_matters.text: The word means useless or unserviceable. The lexicon lists it as the direct opposite of the word for "useful" in this same verse.
The word means useful or serviceable. It is the same word used of Mark in 2 Timothy 4:11, "he is profitable to me for the ministry," so it can describe usefulness in gospel service.
The word means once or formerly. It is used elsewhere for believers' lives before their change, as in 1 Peter 2:10, which sets up the before-and-after contrast here.
This is a strengthened form of "now." It is used for the present time and marks the contrast with Onesimus's past.

takeaway.text: Onesimus had once been useless to Philemon, but now he is useful to Philemon and to Paul. Paul uses that change to ask Philemon to welcome him back as a brother, not just as a servant.

resolved.reason: The cited 2 Timothy 4:11 only says Mark is "profitable to me for the ministry". It does not say Mark was ever "written off". That idea comes from passages (e.g., Acts 15) that are not cited.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
